Transcriptic - Biology’s Robotic Cloud Lab | YesPress
COMPANY PROFILE · 6 MIN READ

Max Hodak had a problem with a button. At Duke, collecting experimental data meant returning to a plate reader every three hours for two days and pressing it. For someone raised on programming, this was an absurd assignment. Software could repeat an instruction indefinitely. Biology required an appointment with a machine. The equipment was expensive; using it could be oddly primitive.

Transcriptic, founded in 2012, grew out of that irritation. Its proposition was easy to grasp: describe an experiment on a computer, let a remote laboratory execute it, and collect the results online. A researcher could retain control of the question while handing over much of the repetitive physical work. The lab, however, would remain stubbornly physical.
The button that would not press itself
“We built a lot from scratch, probably more than we needed.”

Autoprotocol, developed at Transcriptic, gave those instructions a formal language. Volumes, containers and operations could be specified precisely enough for software to interpret. The associated Python library let programmers generate protocols. A separate Transcriptic client, TxPy, exposed projects, runs and datasets through a command line or a Jupyter notebook.

For computational researchers, this connected analysis to execution. For other biologists, programming was another obstacle. The Wet Lab Accelerator research project addressed that gap with a visual interface that translated graphical protocols into instructions for Transcriptic. Easier access required work on both sides of the screen.

In 2016, Brian Naughton documented producing cells expressing an engineered fluorescent protein through Python and Transcriptic. His reported cost was roughly $360, excluding debugging. PCR required repeated iterations; laboratory queues could make each take days. Only three of 50 colonies ultimately appeared to express the intended fluorescent protein.
Minipreps, sequencing

The alternative was familiar: own the instruments, or hire a contract research organization. Emerald Cloud Lab offered another route into remote experimentation. Transcriptic’s appeal lay in combining external laboratory capacity with programmable control. The comparison depended on which methods a researcher needed and how much protocol development remained.

Its product also extended beyond code. In December 2016, Transcriptic and Agilent announced a collaboration to bring genomics reagents into automated workflows, beginning with site-directed mutagenesis. Reagents, methods and machinery had to agree. A neat software abstraction could not substitute for that integration.

Lilly’s Life Sciences Studio made the infrastructure visible. Announced with Strateos in January 2020, the San Diego facility integrated automated chemistry and biology in a remotely controlled laboratory. It emerged from Lilly’s broader $90 million research expansion commitment. That figure was Lilly’s investment program, not the price of a Transcriptic subscription.

Strateos raised a $56.1 million Series B in 2021, led by DCVC and Lux Capital. By April 2023, its announced emphasis had shifted: help customers establish cloud-accessible automated laboratories on their own sites, using LodeStar software and design-and-deployment services. The company cited demand and completed multimillion-dollar design programs for two large biopharmaceutical customers.

The useful move to borrow is modest: find an expensive routine, make its instructions explicit, and test whether shared infrastructure improves the economics. Novel methods, unsupported equipment and protocols dependent on human judgment complicate the calculation. Debugging and waiting belong in the budget alongside reagents.

Transcriptic’s story puts an unusually concrete question to any team promising automation: what, exactly, must happen after the user clicks? The answer includes instruments, scheduling and samples. It also includes the person who decides whether the experiment was worth running.

Today, Transcriptic's products have been re-branded under the Strateos identity. Strateos supports Transcriptic's original users – while simultaneously expanding the platform's capabilities to cloud-based biology and

experimentation. Researchers can remotely submit their experiments, and sit back while our robots do the work. Along the way, they can track the progress of their experiments in real time, allowing them to focus on accelerating discoveries instead of labor-intensive bench work.
Reproducibility is improved with reduced chance of human error, saving time and money while accelerating drug development timelines.
Strateos's software addresses three separate categories of user needs. Several independent web applications provide interfaces for these needs.

The software described above is backed by robotic facilities, capable of carrying out experiments with little to no human intervention. They're akin to data-centers, but the unit of operation being the manipulation of physical samples, instead of computation. Presently, Strateos operates two robotic labs.
We do most of our testing and development at this facility – before rolling out software and hardware improvements to our other labs.
A Design-Forward Product

Over the course of my 3+ years at Transcriptic and Strateos, I've focused on creating a culture of design across the company. The life sciences so often ignore user-centered product development in favor of scientific exploration, and I've made it my charge to ensure that our products are built with a design-centered methodology.
